records.why: Audit item. The lessons gave four partial and partly wrong answers: glands and regions (L3), sphincters as the things that "know" (L6), "genetically programmed" cells (L7) and hormonal and neural signals (L8 only). The accepted account is one story: each enzyme is made by a particular gland and works only on its own substrate and pH, and release is triggered by nerve reflexes (sight, smell, taste and swallowing of food start saliva and gastric juice) and by hormones (gastrin from the stomach, secretin and CCK from the small intestine, which tell the pancreas and gall bladder to act). Checked against the OpenStax chapter section on neural and hormonal regulation. TEACHER DECISION: this goes a little beyond the KICD outcomes, kept to a one-minute teacher explanation in Lesson 3; decide whether to keep it at that depth.

records.new: it 'knows' which chemical to deploy at each stage because each enzyme is made by a specific gland, works only on its own substrate, and is released when nerve signals (the sight, smell and taste of food) and hormones (such as gastrin, secretin and CCK) tell the gland that food has arrived.
records.reference: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, ch. 23.2 Digestive System Processes and Regulation (neural and hormonal controls: gastrin, secretin, CCK)

records.old: The body 'knows' which chemical to release at each stage because each organ's cells are genetically programmed to secrete specific enzymes in response to specific food stimuli (a concept flagged as extending beyond this lesson). Carbohydrates (ugali starch) are partially digested in the mouth and completed in the small intestine; proteins (nyama choma) require the stomach's acid activation of pepsinogen before digestion can begin — explaining why protein digestion takes longer.
records.new: The body 'knows' which chemical to release at each stage because each enzyme is made by a specific gland, works only on its own substrate, and is released when nerve signals and hormones tell the gland that food has arrived (Lesson 3). Carbohydrates (ugali starch) start to be digested in the mouth and are completed in the small intestine; proteins (nyama choma) are not digested in the mouth, begin in the acid stomach once pepsinogen is activated, and are finished in the small intestine — so protein digestion starts later and has more steps than starch digestion.

records.why: A hoe breaks any soil, so it does not show that an enzyme fits one substrate only, and amylase digests all starch, not just maize starch. A padlock and its key do show one-to-one fit. Guideline 6 also asks for the limits of an analogy; they are now stated. TEACHER DECISION: two defensible analogies exist (the teachers chose the jembe, the lesson reflection itself suggests a padlock); confirm you prefer the padlock.
records.old: 'Salivary amylase is like a jembe (hoe) designed only to break up maize starch — it cannot break up the protein fibres in nyama choma. The stomach has a different tool — pepsin — but pepsin only works when HCl makes the stomach very acidic.'
records.new: 'Think of a padlock on a duka door (the food molecule) and the one key that fits it (the enzyme). Salivary amylase is the key that fits starch only, so it cannot open the protein lock in nyama choma. Pepsin is a different key, and it only turns properly when HCl makes the stomach very acidic.' Limits of the analogy, stated to learners: unlike a key, an enzyme is not used up (it works again and again), it speeds up a change rather than opening something, and it stops working if it is too hot or the pH is wrong.
records.group_headline: The jembe (hoe) analogy did not show enzyme specificity (a hoe works on any soil) and had no stated limits; replaced by a padlock-and-key analogy with its limits

records.why: Follows the change of analogy.

records.new: The 'lock-and-key' analogy, told with a padlock and key from a duka door, bridges the abstract concept of enzyme specificity to an everyday object; stating its limits (an enzyme is not used up, and heat or wrong pH stops it) keeps it scientifically accurate.

The notes covered iodine and hot tubes but not the copper-containing Benedict's reagent or the safety of the kerosene stove or hotplate named in the Observe Phase.
records.old: Lab coats or old shirts and safety goggles (or improvised eye protection) are worn throughout.
records.new: Lab coats or old shirts and safety goggles (or improvised eye protection) are worn throughout. Benedict's reagent contains copper(II) sulfate, which is harmful if swallowed and irritates the eyes: keep it away from mouths and rinse spills off skin with water. Put the stove or hotplate on a stable surface away from walkways, and only the teacher handles the hot water bath.

records.why: Teachers had no answer key for the practical, and the lesson did not list substitutes for reagents that many partner schools lack. Expected colours checked against standard school Biology practical guidance: starch gives blue-black with iodine, reducing sugars give green to brick-red with Benedict, ripe banana has little starch left.
records.old: Timer is visible on the board.
records.new: Timer is visible on the board. Expected results, for the teacher to check group tables: iodine test — cooked ugali and raw maize flour blue-black; glucose solution and sukuma wiki extract stay brown-orange; ripe banana weak or no blue-black (most of its starch has become sugar; unripe banana would be strongly blue-black). Benedict's test — glucose brick-red to orange-red; ripe banana orange to brick-red; ugali, maize flour and sukuma wiki stay blue or turn a faint green. If a group's result differs, first ask them to check the sample and the heating time, not the test. Low-cost substitutes: if Benedict's reagent is not available, the teacher can prepare it from copper(II) sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium citrate; if iodine solution is not available, a few drops of tincture of iodine from a pharmacy in a little water will do.

records.old: the small intestine would need to be approximately 2,000 metres long to absorb the same nutrients from our ugali. Because of villi and microvilli, 6 metres is enough.
records.new: the small intestine would need to be roughly 3,600 metres long (6 m × 600) to give the same absorbing surface. Because of villi and microvilli, about 6 metres is enough.
records.why: The script said "up to 600-fold" surface area (Lesson 6 overview and summary) but then "2,000 metres" instead of 600 x 6 m. Recomputed: 6 m x 600 = 3,600 m, and checked a second way: a plain tube of about 3 cm diameter and 6 m long has an inner area near 0.5 m2, and the small intestine absorbing surface is usually given as about 200-300 m2, a ratio of roughly 400-600. The sentence is now an approximate, internally consistent equivalent.
records.reference: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, ch. 23.3 The Small and Large Intestines (folds, villi and microvilli increase surface area about 600-fold)
